results.question: Compare what the book says about making your own chroma keyer with what it says about nons
results.answer:
The short version of the comparison: the book presents the DIY chroma keyer as a worthwhile but ultimately low-value exercise you can build out of color-space math, while it presents nonsquare pixels as a format fact you can't avoid and that carries real workflow hazards. One is about making a tool; the other is about respecting the medium.

| Aspect | Making your own chroma keyer | Nonsquare pixels |
|---|---|---|
| Core idea | Pull a matte by defining color ranges in HSV, since saturation is not an RGB attribute [S3] | Pixels whose width and height differ, so stored and displayed aspect ratios diverge [S5][S8] |
| What the book tells you to do | Convert RGB→HSV, pipe to color curves: RED = Hue, GREEN = Saturation, BLUE = Value, then adjust the three curves to include/exclude the target [S2] | Recognize the format and compensate: unsqueeze the element, transform it (e.g., rotate), then resqueeze it along the x-axis [S14] |
| Authoritative guidance | "An off-the-shelf chroma keyer is hard to improve upon"; building your own is "probably more hassle than it's worth" [S1] | "Double-check everything if you are working with nonsquare pixels" so distortions don't sneak into the final result [S14] |
| Where it shows up | Commercial keyers like Primatte and Keylight; green/blue screens chosen because those hues are absent from skin and hair [S11][S12] | SD video (720×480 NTSC, 720×576 PAL) uses non-square pixels; HD, graphics software, and monitors use square ones; anamorphic/squeezed film formats are the extreme case [S9][S13] |

The two sections differ most in tone and risk. For the DIY keyer, the book gives the full construction recipe — RGB→HSV conversion, the color-curve mapping, and tolerance controls for soft matte edges [S2][S3] — then immediately undercuts it: unlike the luma key, where cleverness can yield real improvements, a homemade chroma keyer is unlikely to beat a commercial one [S1]. The nonsquare-pixel guidance is the reverse: there's nothing to build, and the advice is purely defensive, because the failure is subtle — rotating a 2:1-squeezed Cinemascope element without unsqueezing it first produces a visibly skewed result, and even a 5° rotation shows the problem [S6][S14].

The main intersection is in the compositing pipeline: a chroma keyer operates per-pixel on the stored image, so pixel shape doesn't change which pixels get keyed — but any geometric operation on a keyed element (rotation, scaling, tracking) must account for the squeeze, and the final composite must display at the correct aspect ratio. Notably, the corpus never links the two topics explicitly; that connection is an inference from reading the sections side by side.

results.question: Compare what the book says about miscellaneous drawing tips with what it says about transc
results.answer:
The two topics come from different books in the corpus and sit at opposite ends of the color workflow: the drawing tips are about **choosing colors for beauty**, while transcoding versus color rerendering is about **faithfully converting already-chosen colors between displays**. The drawing tips appear in *Complete Guide to Drawing Dynamic Manga Sword Fighters*, not in a cinema book; the transcoding material is from the *VES Handbook of Visual Effects*.

| Dimension | Drawing tips | Transcoding vs. color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| Question asked | Does the color look right? Is the figure enough? | Will the image look right on a different display? |
| Decision-maker | Artist's taste ("if you feel like the color isn't quite to your liking") | Measured degree of difference between displays |
| Method | Swap colors for a stronger combination; add a luminescence layer for effects | Transcode: linearize RGB → CIE XYZ → target RGB → reapply nonlinearity; or rerender: undo the first display's color rendering, then redo it for the second |
| When to use | Any time before the drawing is finalized | Small differences → transcode; grossly dissimilar black level, white luminance, or viewing conditions → color rerender |
| Nature | Subjective and aesthetic | Objective and colorimetric |

The drawing tips are purely creative: try alternate colors or add bright circles on a new luminescence layer if the illustration feels incomplete [S8]. No measurement is involved — the artist's eye is the only instrument. The VES material is the mirror opposite. Transcoding applies when the two displays match in black level, white luminance, gamma, and viewing conditions and differ only in primary chromaticities — then you linearize the first display's encoded RGB, convert to CIE XYZ, convert to the second display's RGB, and reimpose the encoding nonlinearity [S2]. When contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar, transcoding is not enough: you undo whatever color rendering was done for the first display and color render the CIE XYZ values anew for the second [S1].

These are complementary halves of one pipeline. Color rendering, in color-science terms, is precisely the transformation that accounts for viewing environment — the reason a camera JPEG exposed under desert sunlight is rendered to look correct on an office monitor [S13]. So the drawing tips govern the creative moment of picking colors and effects; transcoding and color rerendering govern the delivery moment of making sure those choices survive the trip to another display.

**Practical implication for cinema:** when footage must play both on a cinema projector and a home display, the black levels, white luminance, and viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar, so the correct move is a full color rerender rather than a simple transcode. When deliverables differ only in primaries (e.g., a Rec. 709 monitor versus an Adobe RGB workflow), a transcode suffices. In both cases, the artist's original decisions — which colors were chosen, which effects added — are the input the transform must preserve faithfully.

results.question: Compare what the book says about transcoding versus color rerendering with what it says ab
results.answer:
The handbook's core distinction is a matter of **how different the two display environments are**. Transcoding is a deterministic numeric conversion for displays that match in everything except color primaries; color rerendering is a perceptual re-doing of the look when the displays are grossly dissimilar.

**Transcoding** (from the VES Handbook) applies when the two displays have identical black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma behavior, and differ only in primary chromaticities. The procedure is purely mathematical: linearize the first display's encoded RGB, convert to CIE XYZ, convert those XYZ values to the second display's RGB, and reimpose the encoding nonlinearity [S5].

**Color rerendering** applies when contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar. Then you must undo whatever color rendering was implicitly or explicitly done for the first display, returning to non-color-rendered CIE XYZ values, and color render those values afresh for the second display [S1]. Color rendering itself is defined as "the transformation of an image to account for differences in viewing environment" — the book's example is a camera JPEG color-rendering a sunlit desert scene for an office monitor with far lower peak white luminance [S4].

| | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| **When used** | Displays match in everything but primaries | Black/white levels or viewing conditions grossly dissimilar |
| **Assumption** | Same black level, white luminance, conditions, gamma | First display's rendering must be undone first |
| **Operation** | Linearize → XYZ → second RGB → reimpose nonlinearity | Undo rendering → re-render XYZ for second display |
| **Character** | Deterministic numeric conversion | Perceptual, look-defining transformation |

The surrounding chapters reinforce the same split: camera raw defers color rendering downstream because it can be done by the VFX team, whereas a baked-in non-raw render is hard to undo [S3]; and the ACES workflow separates the artistic look (RRT) from per-display delivery (ODT), with gamut mapping flagged as the remaining problem when delivering to a low-gamut device like HDTV [S12].

**FACE OFF**: the retrieved evidence contains no treatment of FACE OFF at all — no passage names the film, a face-swap process, or any technique by that name. The nearest material is a compositing passage on morphing a face to non-face targets like a car or baseball [S11], and a description of the "Face of Code" FACS platform [S2], neither of which engages the transcoding-versus-rerendering distinction. So the comparison you're after can't be grounded in the corpus; the missing piece is any FACE OFF content in the source material.

results.answer:
The corpus gives a rich, machine-checkable account of **affect, fatigue, and injury as control states**, but it contains no retrievable treatment of the film *Face/Off* — the only place the film could appear is the Dancyger filmography, and the retrieved pages don't include the entry. So the comparison's film side is missing, and that missing premise is worth naming before looking at the control-state framework.

## What the handbook says: affect, fatigue, and injury as control states

The handbook's section 6.1, the canonical JSON, and the combat-state metric table all treat these three as **persistent state** that must be declared, caused, and repaid in observable behavior:

| State | Declared as | What must hold | Failure signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Affect** | beliefs with confidence and truth status [S6] | every declared affect change produces at least one visible or tactical consequence [S13] | "emotion appears only in label or face" [S13] |
| **Fatigue** | global exertion (RPE, breath cycle, recovery rate) plus per-limb local capacity [S3][S6] | taxed regions alter later capacity, variability, timing, or tactics [S13] | exertion never changes later action [S13] |
| **Injury** | region, pain, severity, mechanical effects, compensations, confidence [S2][S6] | effects and compensations persist; injured regions must not perform at baseline [S13] | injury vanishes or acts at baseline without cause [S5][S13] |

The design logic is explicit. For fatigue, the handbook even proposes a compiler-style update — `f(t+Δt) = clamp(f(t) + work + impact − recovery, 0, 1)` — while warning that those terms must be calibrated, "not inferred reliably from prose alone" [S4]. For injury, the model is deliberately flagged as "dramatic annotation, not clinical measurement," with a confidence value attached [S2]. The specimen fight binds the persistence rule into prose: "Mara's right-shoulder injury begins at state.v2 and persists through the final frame" [S5].

The stagecraft books in the corpus voice the same principle for performers: an attack should change "mood or functionality… for the rest of the scene" [S8], pain reads through asymmetry and involuntary contortion rather than matched, natural positions [S9], and exhaustion is one of the canonical fight emotions ("I am exhausted and feel my energy is waning"; "I must strive to hide the effort") [S7]. The handbook's control-state idea is essentially a formalization of that acting rule — state must persist and leak into action. (Note that *Making Meaning with Machines* uses "state" differently: Laban-derived Effort states — combinations of weight, space, time, and flow effort [S1] — not affect/fatigue/injury.)

results.question: Compare what the book says about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states with what
results.answer:
The corpus treats these as two different explanatory levels: affect, fatigue, and injury are **internal control states** that cause movement, while an object's movement against a background is a **perceptual relation** that viewers read from movement. One answers "why does the body move this way," the other answers "what does that motion look like and mean to an observer."

| | Affect / fatigue / injury as control states | Movement of an object with a background |
|---|---|---|
| Framing | Causal, generative, stateful | Perceptual, relational, optical |
| Core claims | States must change later action selection and execution; "not adjectives appended after choreography is chosen" [S6] | Motion is defined relative to surroundings: induced movement transfers motion to a nearby stationary object, so the stationary object appears to move [S2] |
| Content | Appraisal updates (valence, arousal, dominance), global/local fatigue capacity, injury mechanics and compensations [S1][S6][S15] | Quality affinity, motion parallax as a time-integrated depth cue, camera-vs-object motion separability, Z-depth compositing limits [S8][S14][S12] |
| Validation | Metrics like affect-to-action coupling, fatigue propagation, injury-compensation consistency [S13] | Perceptual caveats: Z-depth fails on transparent/live-action elements [S12], depth staging must be judged through time [S14] |

**Control states: internal and forward-looking.** The handbook defines affect through appraisal updates — an event is scored on goal congruence, controllability, and certainty, which shift valence/arousal/dominance and then alter behavior, e.g., attention narrowing, urgent recovery, higher risk tolerance [S3][S6]. Fatigue is both global (RPE, breath cycle, recovery rate) and local per limb, producing coordination effects like wider step-width variability [S15]. Injury specifies mechanical consequences (load acceptance, flexion tolerance), compensations (favoring the right leg, shortening stance), and an uncertainty label [S1]. Each state has required fields and an update trigger in the combat-state schema [S5], and the coupling metrics exist specifically to catch states that "appear only in label or face" or regions that perform at baseline without cause [S13].

**Object and background: external and perceptual.** Bruce Block's material describes induced movement, where the perceived movers swap depending on the surrounding reference — the moving object can appear stationary while the background appears to move [S2]. Quality operates the same way: low visual intensity when object movement shares direction and curve across shots [S8]. The compositing evidence extends this: motion parallax is a time-integrated depth cue, so depth staging must be evaluated across time rather than in one frame [S14]; camera and object trajectories are separable controls [S14]; and Z-depth compositing breaks down on partially transparent elements, where a pixel receives color from both foreground and background [S12].

**Where they meet.** Both frameworks insist the same thing: movement is never self-contained. For the handbook, movement parameters (acceleration profile, posture amplitude, gaze allocation, willingness to accept unstable support [S3]) are the output of internal states plus their compensations; for the visual sources, the same parameters only acquire meaning relative to a background. A consequence for design: an affect or injury state changes the body, but an audience reads that change through induced movement, parallax, and quality contrast — so the control-state layer and the background staging layer have to be modeled consistently or the perceived story will contradict the simulated body state. Note that these claims come from different source strands in the corpus (the CPCS handbook versus The Visual Story and compositing literature), so the comparison is between complementary levels of description rather than two rival theories of the same phenomenon.

results.question: Compare what the book says about movement of an object with a background with what it says
results.answer:
Both topics answer the same underlying question — how to keep a foreground element believably connected to a background across a cut — but the books treat the visual problem as a technical calibration task and the sound problem as a perceptual, judgment-driven craft.

**What the visual side says.** The VES Handbook frames object–background movement as **match moving**: when the foreground camera moves, the background must move appropriately, so tracking data is extracted from the foreground image and applied to the background during compositing [S9]. In virtual-studio work, that matched movement is automated once the system is set up and calibrated, with the blended result mixed in real time [S11]. The principle is exact correspondence — the background is not free to behave independently.

**What the sound side says.** The editing texts emphasize continuity of sound and its perspective as critical: levels should match the on-screen proximity and narrative importance of their sources [S4], a close-up's louder whistle reflects the magnified visual size [S6], and a diegetic sound like an overhead airplane should carry across the cut into the next shot even if the plane is no longer visible, usually at a slightly lowered volume [S7]. Background ambience (walla) is deliberately kept on separate tracks precisely so it can run continuously through multiple cuts and blend them [S3]. And because the ear registers an abrupt sound cut more readily than a graduated change, ambience mismatches are fixed by augmenting quieter tracks and transitioning via sound dissolves rather than hard cuts [S12]. The sound editor thinks both horizontally (one sound after another) and vertically (layers happening simultaneously) [S10].

| | Object–background movement | Sound editing |
|---|---|---|
| Core problem | Background must move as the foreground moves | Sound must stay consistent with visual perspective |
| Method | Tracking data extracted, applied to background | Editor's ear: levels, layering, dissolves |
| Continuity device | Calibrated, automated matched movement | Walla/ambience carried over cuts, J-cuts/dissolves |
| Handling change | Background follows foreground exactly | Gradual changes; abrupt cuts are flagged as errors [S12] |

The two bodies of advice agree on the central requirement: continuity at the cut, with the background subordinate to the foreground — visually it must mirror the foreground's motion, aurally it must mirror the foreground's proximity and remain present even when off-screen [S7]. They part on method: the visual solution is data-driven and once calibrated runs automatically, while the audio solution is never automated — it rests on the editor's judgment about levels, layering, and gradual transitions. One caveat: the visual material comes from a single source (the VES Handbook), while the sound material spans several texts, so this is a comparison of topics across books rather than one book's unified doctrine.

results.question: Compare what the book says about sound editing with what it says about write radio sparely
results.answer:
Both bodies of advice preach the same doctrine of restraint, but from opposite ends of the production chain: writing radio sparely subtracts words before anything is recorded, while sound editing subtracts and reshapes sound after recording.

| Aspect | Writing radio sparely | Sound editing |
|---|---|---|
| Core principle | Bare-bones script; silence is "to radio what white space is to print" | No more dialogue than absolutely necessary; cleanest signal possible |
| Material worked on | Words on a page | Recorded dialogue, wild sound, SFX, music tracks |
| Point in the process | Writing, before production | Post-production: rough assembly → fine cut |
| Signature technique | Voice talent reading slowly, quietly, one word at a time | Splitting tracks, replacing words, balancing levels, re-recording wild sound |
| Danger to avoid | Overdoing sound effects | Unintentional degradation of the signal |
| End goal | A simple, clean, easy-to-comprehend core message | Believability, atmosphere, character credibility, emotional music |

The convergence is striking. The sound editor is told to use "no more dialog than is absolutely necessary," [S12] and the radio writer is told to write sparely unless the concept genuinely demands fast action and many words [S3]. Both treat absence as a tool: silence in radio "enlarges the idea it surrounds," [S2] and dialogue editing achieves a similar effect by removing unwanted sounds and balancing what remains [S10]. Both also demand deliberate control — the sound editor should start with the cleanest, strongest signal and degrade it only as a conscious effect, [S5] just as the spare radio script lets the voice talent slow down so each word lands [S3].

The differences come down to craft and timing. Radio-spare writing is a compositional act: choosing fewer words, trusting the audience, and leaving air for the idea to expand [S2][S3]. Sound editing is a reshaping act on finished recordings: splitting dialogue onto separate tracks, replacing individual words, balancing clip levels, [S10] and working from a rough cut aimed at believability toward a fine cut where dramatic emphasis, metaphor, atmosphere, and a music track are added [S8][S12]. Even their relationship to sound effects inverts: radio writing warns against overusing them, [S7] while sound editing treats them as raw material to collect and exploit — a car door slam re-recorded close-mic, or the clean recording of a spoon stirring tea in *Get Out* [S11].

One framing note: these are two different streams of advice rather than one book speaking twice. The radio guidance comes from advertising copywriting texts like *Hey Whipple Squeeze This* and the Adweek handbook, which call radio writing a rare, "pure" form of writing built on language; [S1][S14][S15] the sound-editing guidance comes from film and TV editing texts. They happen to agree on subtraction — but they practice it on different materials, at opposite ends of the timeline.

results.question: Compare what the book says about write radio sparely with what it says about rewards of go
results.answer:
The comparison is between two different books, not one: **Hey Whipple Squeeze This** sets out a craft rule for radio copywriting, while **Gifts Differing** (Myers & Myers) makes a psychological claim about personality type. The first has rich evidence; the second rests on a single passage.

**Write radio sparely** is a negative discipline — subtract until the idea stands alone. Bare-bones execution "leaps out of the radio," and silence functions as white space does in print, enlarging the idea it surrounds [S1]. Sparsity lets voice talent read slowly, quietly, one word at a time [S2], and it protects the concept from the time-eating promotional tags clients add to spots [S3]. The practical method is to write the mandatories first, time them, and fit the commercial into what's left; overwriting is called the most common mistake in radio, so the rule is "be a genius. Underwrite" [S4].

**Good type development**, in contrast, is an additive discipline — building out one's natural personality type. The book's claim is that type development is a variable with a wide range and a profound influence on **effectiveness, success, happiness, and mental health** [S9].

| Dimension | Write radio sparely | Good type development |
|---|---|---|
| Source | Hey Whipple Squeeze This | Gifts Differing |
| Kind of claim | Craft principle for copywriting | Psychological-developmental claim |
| Mechanism | Subtract words, add silence | Develop the full range of one's type |
| Payoff | A spot that fits, breathes, and lands | Influence on effectiveness, success, happiness, mental health |
| Scope of reward | The individual commercial | The whole life |

The two share a core logic: **restraint or discipline in the medium shapes the outcome**. Sparse writing is the disciplined use of silence to make a 30- or 60-second idea stronger; type development is the disciplined development of a personality's capacities to make a life stronger. The contrast is in scale and direction — radio advice is subtractive and its reward is immediate and concrete (a spot that works), while type development is growth-oriented and its reward is broad and long-term (a life that works). One caveat: the evidence on type development is a single excerpt, so the second half of this comparison is necessarily thinner than the first [S9].
